summary: A humorous April 1 memo written as a historical look back at the usage of an imaginary IP version 9. It is a joke, not a protocol specification.

eli5.summary: A made-up history lesson about a pretend Internet version. It is for laughs.

subtitle: A humorous future history of an imaginary IP Version 9

tldr.problem: It is April 1st, 1994. What if we look back from the far future at how well IP Version 9 worked?
tldr.mechanism: This RFC imagines that IPv9 took over the Internet, offering hierarchical addressing with 42 levels of routing, vastly larger address space, and ubiquitous addressing of everything from light switches to implanted medical devices to interplanetary networks.
tldr.outcome: This is an April 1st RFC—it is pure fiction. No such protocol exists. But it is a humorous exploration of what happened after IPv4 address space exhaustion, poking fun at both unrealistic hopes and real concerns.

facts.label: Fictional broadcast mechanism
facts.value: Directed broadcast queries (e.g., to all cardboard packages)

today: This is an April 1st RFC and is not a real protocol. No IPv9 exists. The memo is a humorous speculative history, and its real value lies in the social commentary on ubiquitous computing and privacy buried beneath the jokes.

sections.title: The April 1st Premise
sections.content: This memo is published on April 1st, 1994, and frames itself as a historical look back at IP Version 9. The conceit: it is now sometime after 2023, address exhaustion forced a change from IPv4, and now we are reviewing how IPv9 fared. The memo explores imaginary uses of IPv9 in routing, allocation, manufacture, and applications—all wildly speculative and humorous.
sections.eli5: It is April 1st, so imagine we had a different Internet protocol in the future, and let's pretend to remember how it worked.

sections.title: The Vast Address Space and Hierarchy
sections.content:
IPv9 supposedly has 42 levels of hierarchical routing, allowing every conceivable device to have its own network assignment. Commercial Internet providers could hand out 1 billion addresses per house. The routing hierarchy permits levels to be reassigned dynamically, unlike the fixed fields in earlier designs. The address space is so enormous that light switches, mains sockets, and sub-chip nanocode can each have their own address.

The memo jokes that even this is running short, due to the discovery of intelligent life on other solar systems and the need for world-size address spaces at level 3, galaxy-wide networks at level 2, and inter-galaxy routing at level 1. The hardest problem now is how to handle parallel universes.
sections.eli5: Every single device—even tiny ones—can have an address. There are so many addresses that you could give billions to each house and still not run out... mostly.

sections.title: Imaginary IPv9 Applications
sections.content:
The memo spins humorous tales of IPv9 use cases. Body monitors implanted in the bloodstream send SNMP trap messages when organs fail—until the crosstalk and broadcast storms cause patients to go into violent spasms. IPv9 addressable consumer packaging allows companies to query products for usage data ("All cardboard packages, report in"), but consumers fear invasion of privacy. An IPv9 magazine answers questions about its own contents. The paper jokes about "sneakernet" shoes from Skholl that forward foot odor analysis to manufacturers.

The underlying theme: vast address space enables ubiquitous connectivity, but not all uses are welcome.
sections.eli5: We could network everything—even your socks and your sandwich wrapper. But that does not mean you would want every maker watching where you go and what you eat.

sections.title: The Joke and the Lesson
sections.content: The memo concludes with the adage "Those who do not study history, are doomed to repeat it." The message, delivered straight-faced through absurdist speculation, is actually a warning: we need to think carefully about scalability, privacy, and real-world consequences of design choices, not just about raw address space and hierarchical capability. The humor masks a serious point about the need for cautious engineering.
sections.eli5: The joke is funny, but it is also pointing out real problems: we need to think about what we are doing, not just dream big.
